## Tours featuring Anakena, Rano Raraku, and Ahu Tongariki: an archaeological day on Rapa Nui

On [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), many archaeological sites lie along different parts of the coast. A full day of sightseeing can include the places where moai were carved, major ceremonial platforms, and a shoreline associated with the island's early settlement history. This is the sequence offered by the [Anakena, Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki excursion](/chile/easter-island/anakena-rano-raraku-tongariki-tour/).

This catalog brings together {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include the excursion as part of a longer journey. When choosing, consider more than the number of stone statues: account for travel time between sites, the other days spent on Rapa Nui, and flights between the island and mainland Chile.

## What one day along the southern and eastern coasts offers

The itinerary begins at [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/), an archaeological complex associated with legends about Hotu Matu'a. The next major stop is the [Rano Raraku volcano](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/). Its quarry reveals where the statues were carved and why some moai remain on the hillside in various stages of completion.

You then reach [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), where 15 moai stand on a restored platform. This is a different kind of monument: Rano Raraku shows how the statues were made, while Tongariki demonstrates their role in the island's ceremonial architecture. Comparing the two adds more meaning than a simple list of stops.

The itinerary also includes the [Poike Peninsula](/chile/place/poike-peninsula/), [Ahu Te Pito Kura](/chile/place/ahu-te-pito-kura/), and [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/). At Anakena, natural scenery meets historic monuments. After the excursion, the group returns to [Hanga Roa](/chile/place/hanga-roa/).

| Stop | Main interest |
|---|---|
| Ahu Akahanga | Ancient ceremonial ruins |
| Rano Raraku | The moai quarry |
| Ahu Tongariki | A platform with 15 statues |
| Anakena | Beach and cultural landscape |

This standalone excursion is confirmed as a **full-day outing** with an **included boxed lunch**. Other terms of a specific tour, such as transport and accommodation, should be checked in that tour's itinerary: the excursion itself does not describe the entire travel package.

## How the archaeological day fits into different itineraries

On the [17-day private grand tour of Chile, Argentina and Brazil](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/), Day 4 is devoted to the full-day excursion to Rano Raraku and Anakena. Before that, guests arrive on Rapa Nui and explore [Rano Kau and Orongo](/chile/easter-island/orongo-rano-kau-tour/). After the main archaeological day comes a morning excursion to [Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai](/chile/easter-island/easter-island-akivi-puna-pau-tahai/), followed by the return to Santiago.

This option is suited to travelers who want to experience the island's monuments as part of a broader journey. After Rapa Nui, the itinerary continues through the Atacama, Patagonia, Mendoza, Iguazu, and Buenos Aires. However, its busy schedule means that island time is divided into prearranged sightseeing days.

The excursion is also included as a linked module in the [14-day Peru, Bolivia and Chile journey](/multi-country/tour/south-america-peru-bolivia-chile-easter-island/). When comparing programs, check the actual sequence of island visits and flights: a major continental tour should not automatically be treated as equivalent to a separate multi-day Rapa Nui stay.

If the island itself is your priority, compare the [3-day “Easter Island: Moai and Volcanoes” tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/). It visits Rano Raraku, Tongariki and Anakena on Day 2, while Rano Kau and Orongo are covered on another sightseeing day. It is a separate itinerary even though the key sites overlap.

## What to know before visiting Rano Raraku and Tongariki

Rapa Nui is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The national park's archaeological areas have monument-protection rules: visitors must stay on authorized paths, maintain the required distance from moai and platforms, and refrain from touching stone structures.

Under the park's published rules, an entrance ticket and an accredited guide are required. Rano Raraku is one of the sites allowing only **one visit per ticket**. This matters when planning several days on the island: you cannot assume unlimited returns to the quarry whenever convenient.

For a comfortable full day, bring suitable shoes, protection from sun and wind, drinking water, and enough free storage on your phone or camera. An oceanfront stop does not turn the whole day into a beach holiday: the archaeological itinerary remains the focus, and swimming depends on the arrangements of the specific tour.

## Choosing an itinerary that includes this excursion

If moai are your main interest, choose a trip that allows several consecutive days on the island. Then the main route to Tongariki can be complemented by the [ceremonial village of Orongo](/chile/place/orongo-village/) and the western monuments, without flights consuming most of your only day.

If you want to explore South America more broadly, compare the length of the island stay with the mainland itinerary. On a grand tour, Rapa Nui is one of several cultural and natural regions; on a shorter island-focused tour, its monuments take up most of the journey. For alternatives, browse the [full Chile tour catalog](/chile/tour/) and [Chile's cultural and historical itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/chile/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours featuring Anakena and Tongariki

### How long is the excursion to Rano Raraku and Tongariki?

The standalone Ada Tours excursion lasts **a full day**. It visits several widely separated archaeological sites and finishes near Anakena Beach.

### What is the difference between Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki?

[Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/) is the site where moai were carved, with unfinished statues still present. [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/) is a restored ceremonial platform with 15 standing statues.

### Can I visit Rano Raraku again the next day?

Under current park rules, Rano Raraku permits **one visit per ticket**. It is best to plan it as a complete stop and agree the sightseeing day in advance.

### Do I need a separate guide to visit the monuments?

Visits to national park sites require an accredited guide. The arrangements for the guide, tickets, and transport should be checked against the tour you select.

## Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai: three chapters in Rapa Nui's history

[Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/) contains hundreds of archaeological monuments, each revealing a different aspect of Polynesian culture. This Ada Tours excursion brings together three stories: the **seven moai of Ahu Akivi**, the production of red stone headpieces at Puna Pau, and the ceremonial platforms of the Tahai complex.

The route also includes the unrestored **Hanga Pikure ahu**. This is a standalone cultural excursion; it does not automatically include the southern coastline, Tongariki, or Anakena Beach.

## Ahu Akivi: seven statues in the island's interior

[Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/) is a restored ceremonial platform bearing **seven moai**. According to local tradition, the figures are associated with seven scouts sent to Rapa Nui by King Hotu Matu'a. The story occupies an important place in the island's cultural memory.

Ahu Akivi is located in the central part of Rapa Nui, giving it a different setting from the many coastal platforms. The landscape is especially apparent here: open grassland, gentle rises, and imposing statues facing the horizon.

Restored monuments show how ceremonial architecture may have appeared, but the reconstruction is based on archaeological work. The site must be treated as protected historical heritage.

## Hanga Pikure: an unrestored platform

The next site is **Hanga Pikure ahu**, identified in the itinerary as an unrestored platform. It allows visitors to compare archaeological monuments in different states of preservation.

Where figures have been raised onto pedestals again, visitors see a reconstructed picture of a complex. At unrestored ahu, traces of damage and changes in the island's history are more visible. The comparison gives the walk added depth: Rapa Nui's past is far more complex than rows of identical standing statues.

## Puna Pau: the origins of the red pukao

[Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/) is a volcanic area where reddish stone was quarried to make **pukao**, stone elements placed on the heads of some moai.

This red volcanic rock differs from the material used to carve most of the statues. Puna Pau therefore helps explain how the monuments were made and embellished: some quarries supplied the figures, while others provided individual decorative and symbolic elements.

You can see traces of ancient work and unfinished pieces here. For understanding the island's archaeology, this site is no less interesting than the restored statues beside the sea.

## Tahai: a coastal ceremonial complex

[Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/) comprises several historic platforms. Here you can see **Ko Te Riku, Tahai and Vai Uri**. Ko Te Riku is known for a moai with reconstructed eyes, which help visitors imagine how a statue appeared in its ceremonial setting.

The coastal location makes the relationship between the platforms and their surroundings particularly clear. These monuments were not isolated decorative sculptures: they belonged to the social and ritual life of local communities.

Tahai completes the narrative of the excursion. After the seven statues at Ahu Akivi and the workshop area at Puna Pau, travelers see how the sculptures became part of sacred ceremonial places.

## How this excursion differs from the southern route

The Akivi — Puna Pau — Tahai itinerary focuses on **ceremonial platforms, the production of pukao, and ritual architecture**. A separate [southern-coast excursion with a private picnic at Anakena](/chile/easter-island/easter-island-south-coast-anakena-private-picnic/) covers Rano Raraku, Tongariki, and time at the beach.

The two experiences complement each other without duplicating their stops. If you want to see most of the island's cultural sites, plan the visits on separate days while respecting national park requirements.

The excursion's price, exact duration, and included entrance tickets should be agreed when selecting the trip. Island monuments must be treated with care, and authorized routes must be followed.

## Frequently asked questions about Ahu Akivi and Tahai

### How many moai stand at Ahu Akivi?

**Seven** restored statues.

### What are pukao?

Red stone elements placed on the heads of some moai. They were made from volcanic rock quarried in the Puna Pau area.

### Does the route include Anakena Beach?

No. Anakena is part of a different excursion along the island's southern coast.

### Which platforms are part of the Tahai complex?

Ko Te Riku, Tahai and Vai Uri.

## Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai: a morning excursion on Rapa Nui

**This excursion visits three sites that reveal the history of the moai stone statues.** On [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), travelers will see a restored platform with seven figures, a quarry for red volcanic rock, and ceremonial sites overlooking the ocean.

We offer this as a private morning excursion. It includes [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), [Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), and [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/). The exact duration, transfer arrangements, and access conditions are agreed for each trip.

The itinerary is particularly rewarding if you have already seen photographs of the famous moai but would like to understand how these sculptures relate to ceremonial platforms, local stone, and Rapa Nui beliefs about ancestors.

## Ahu Akivi: seven statues and a local legend

[Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/) is known for **seven moai** standing together on one platform. Local tradition associates them with scouts who arrived on the island before later settlement. This is part of the island's cultural heritage and should be distinguished from archaeological evidence of how the monument was constructed.

The site is striking for its setting and composition. The seven figures form a single ensemble, and their orientation within the landscape differs from that of many coastal platforms. The monument was restored in the 20th century, so visitors see a carefully reconstructed archaeological site rather than an accidental group of stones.

While there, look at the platform's shape, how the figures are arranged, and the material from which they were carved. Most of the island's monumental moai were made from volcanic tuff. Producing and transporting them required organized labor and specialized knowledge, and researchers continue to study the precise ancient techniques.

## Puna Pau: where the moai's red “hats” came from

[Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/) is a quarry for red volcanic rock. It was used to make cylindrical ornaments known as *pukao*, which can be seen on the heads of some moai.

The red stone is different from the main rock used for most statues. Visiting the quarry helps show that the work of the island's craftspeople took place in different locations: the stone bodies of the moai and their headpieces came from different sources.

Archaeologists and cultural researchers still debate the exact symbolism of pukao. They are often described as headwear or hairstyles and are also associated with social status. For visitors, the key is to see where the material was extracted and understand why moving these heavy stone elements posed a separate challenge.

## Tahai: ceremonial platforms by the ocean

[Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/) is made up of several restored ceremonial platforms. The published excursion specifically highlights Ko Te Riku, a moai with reconstructed eyes.

The experience here differs from Ahu Akivi. The proximity of the ocean and the arrangement of the ceremonial space demonstrate how architecture connected with the island's landscape and community life.

Ko Te Riku's eyes are particularly important to the sculpture's appearance. Their reconstruction helps visitors imagine how some moai might have looked during ceremonial use, although a modern reconstruction should not be mistaken for an exact record of an ancient ritual.

| Monument | What you will see |
|---|---|
| Ahu Akivi | Seven moai on a platform |
| Puna Pau | The red-stone quarry |
| Tahai | Coastal ceremonial platforms |

## Preparing for the excursion

Rapa Nui's archaeological monuments lie within a protected national park that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Visits are subject to access rules, movement restrictions, and requirements to protect the stone structures. Current entry and guiding arrangements should be checked against the park's rules.

Comfortable closed-toe shoes are useful on uneven ground; sunscreen and a windproof jacket help in the island's exposed landscape. Stone statues and platforms must not be touched or used as supports for photographs.

This morning route is different from the island's other excursions, such as the Rano Raraku quarry, Ahu Tongariki, and the ceremonial village of Orongo. Those sites are not among this product's three stops and require a separate itinerary.

If this is your first visit to [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), consider combining the excursion with other historical sites. More trips exploring Latin America's heritage are listed under [culture and history](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about Ahu Akivi and Tahai

### How many moai stand at Ahu Akivi?

The restored Ahu Akivi platform has **7 moai**.

### What is Puna Pau?

It is a quarry of red volcanic rock used to make pukao ornaments for some of the island's statues.

### How is Tahai different from Ahu Akivi?

Tahai is an oceanfront ceremonial complex with several platforms. Ahu Akivi is best known for its single ensemble of seven statues.

### Can I visit the monuments independently?

Some national park sites have mandatory guide and access requirements. These should be confirmed for your visit date; the private format of our excursion does not override the rules of the protected area.

## Tours featuring Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai: three monuments in one morning

[Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), the [Puna Pau quarry](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), and [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/) reveal different aspects of the history of the moai on Easter Island. Here, visitors can see statues standing on a platform, the source of stone used for red headpieces, and a restored coastal ceremonial complex.

The [Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai excursion](/chile/easter-island/easter-island-akivi-puna-pau-tahai/) is offered as a private morning outing. Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include it as part of a longer journey. More than the list of sites matters: this route should be considered alongside excursions to the southern and eastern coasts, as well as the onward flight schedule.

## What you can see at the three monuments

**[Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/).** Seven moai stand on the platform. According to local legend, they are associated with scouts who arrived before Hotu Matu'a. The site is a good introduction to the positioning of statues in the landscape: it is not part of the coastal complex where Tongariki is usually photographed.

**[Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/).** This quarry of red volcanic tuff supplied cylindrical stone headpieces called *pukao*, which can be seen on some moai. It highlights another aspect of the ancient craftspeople's work. The main bodies of many statues were carved at [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), while their headpieces were made from a different stone.

**[Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/).** An archaeological complex with restored platforms beside the ocean. One of its best-known statues is Ko Te Riku, whose eyes have been reconstructed. Tahai lets visitors see moai in the context of ceremonial structures rather than as isolated museum sculptures.

| Site | Main question |
|---|---|
| Ahu Akivi | Why do seven moai stand together? |
| Puna Pau | Where did the stone for pukao come from? |
| Tahai | What did a ceremonial complex look like? |

These three stops form a standalone themed excursion. Its exact duration in hours, entrance-ticket prices, and included transfers have not yet been specified. The terms should be determined according to the particular tour that includes the excursion.

## Where this excursion fits into a longer journey

On the [17-day private grand tour of Chile, Argentina and Brazil](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/), the outing to Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau and Tahai takes place on **Day 5**. Earlier days are dedicated to [Rano Kau and Orongo](/chile/easter-island/orongo-rano-kau-tour/) and [Rano Raraku, Ahu Tongariki and Anakena](/chile/easter-island/anakena-rano-raraku-tongariki-tour/).

After the morning excursion on Day 5, the itinerary calls for a return flight from Easter Island to Santiago by private charter, taking approximately 5.5 hours. Guests spend the night in Chile's capital, and the following day fly to Calama and continue to San Pedro de Atacama. **This tour does not promise a direct flight from Easter Island to the Atacama.**

That is a significant consideration. For travelers who want to see Rapa Nui's key monuments and then explore several South American regions, this morning provides a logical end to the island stay. Those wishing to explore the archaeological sites at a slower pace should consider an extra day on the island rather than scheduling a complicated flight immediately after the excursion.

## How this route differs from other Rapa Nui excursions

[Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/) and [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/) generally take a substantial part of a full day because of their major ceremonial structures and quarry areas. This itinerary brings [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), [Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), and [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/) together in a separate morning excursion focused on seven statues, pukao stone, and restored platforms.

Another distinct story is the birdman tradition at [Orongo](/chile/place/orongo-village/) near [Rano Kau](/chile/place/rano-kau-volcano/). It belongs to a different historical practice on Rapa Nui. It is therefore better to choose a tour that spreads the monuments over several sightseeing days than to try to squeeze everything into one extended stop.

## Practical visiting arrangements

Rapa Nui National Park sites require an entrance ticket and an accredited guide. Visitors must remain on authorized routes and keep their distance from platforms, moai, and archaeological objects. Current access rules for individual sites should be taken into account when finalizing the order of visits.

Comfortable closed-toe footwear and clothing suitable for windy weather are appropriate for the morning outing. If it is combined with a flight the same day, the actual excursion finish time, time to collect luggage, and journey to the airport are especially important. The name of the excursion alone does not establish how long each stop lasts or whether tickets are available.

If you are comparing other [Chile tours](/chile/tour/), first check the number of nights on [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), then review the sites scheduled for each day. Relevant terms are usually detailed in the [full 17-day grand tour itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/).

### Is Ahu Akivi the same as Ahu Tongariki?

No. [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/) is known for its platform with seven moai. [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/) is a different site with 15 restored statues.

### What makes Puna Pau interesting?

At [Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), red volcanic tuff was quarried to make stone pukao headpieces for some moai.

Ada Tours describes it as a **morning** excursion. The exact number of hours is not specified separately; on the 17-day tour, a flight to Santiago follows it.

The excursion has its own [itinerary page](/chile/easter-island/easter-island-akivi-puna-pau-tahai/). Independent arrangements, transport, entrance tickets, and guiding should be discussed for the particular request.

## Easter Island in a day: the southern coast, moai, and a picnic at Anakena

[Rapa Nui](/chile/place/easter-island/) is best known for its stone **moai** statues and ceremonial platforms called *ahu*. This Ada Tours excursion is designed as a **full-day** experience, combining important archaeological monuments along the southern coast with relaxation by the ocean.

The route visits Ahu Vaihu at Hanga Te'e Bay, Ahu Akahanga, the [Rano Raraku volcano](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), Te Pito Kura, and [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) with its Nau Nau platform. The final part of the day includes a **private picnic**.

## Vaihu and Akahanga: early ceremonial sites

Along the southern coast, travelers explore the unrestored platforms of **Ahu Vaihu** and **Ahu Akahanga**. They are especially interesting because they show archaeological monuments in a different condition from restored platforms with statues raised back into position.

According to local tradition, Akahanga is linked to the legendary first king Hotu Matu'a. Such stories are important to the island's cultural memory, but should be understood as traditional accounts rather than proven archaeological facts.

Look closely at the stonework and the surrounding coastal landscape. The platforms were connected to the social and ritual life of Rapa Nui and today provide an insight into its historic setting beyond the island's most familiar postcard scenes.

## Rano Raraku: where the moai were carved

[Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/) is the ancient quarry where most moai were carved. Hundreds of figures remain on its slopes, in different stages of carving and transportation. This is where it is easiest to appreciate the labor-intensive process of producing enormous stone sculptures.

Around Rano Raraku, approximately **397 statues are counted on the slopes**, while the total number of moai on the island is estimated at around **900**. These are approximate archaeological estimates, not a fixed inventory of figures always accessible to visitors.

The quarry is valuable for more than the number of moai. It reveals the process: some figures remain embedded in rock, others have been partly detached, and still others stand on the slopes. A visit helps explain where the statues on the coastal platforms came from.

## Ahu Tongariki: fifteen moai in a row

The next stop is [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), the island's largest restored ceremonial platform. **15 moai** stand here in a line. On the exposed coastline, they are especially impressive against the volcanic terrain and the ocean.

Restoration returned the platform to its recognizable appearance, but it remains a protected archaeological monument. Visitors must not touch the statues, climb onto the platforms, or cross the permitted boundaries.

## Te Pito Kura and Anakena: finishing by the ocean

After Tongariki, you continue to Ahu Te Pito Kura and the Te Pito o te Henua stone, associated in local tradition with the idea of the “Navel of the World.”

The final stop is near [Anakena](/chile/place/anakena-beach/), a beach of pale sand, palm trees, and turquoise water. It is also home to **Ahu Nau Nau**, another well-known archaeological complex.

At the end of the day, there is time to walk and swim, and the excursion includes a **private picnic overlooking the coast**. Swimming depends on sea conditions and any restrictions in force. The picnic is included, but the menu and availability of drinks have not been specified in advance.

## Excursion arrangements and national park rules

Rapa Nui is a protected cultural landscape. Routes around archaeological sites, guiding requirements, and access to individual areas must be checked against the national park's current rules.

This is a **full-day** excursion. The price, included entrance tickets, guide language, and exact meeting time have not yet been specified. They should be agreed before the trip.

The excursion suits travelers who want to spend a full day exploring archaeological monuments and finish on the beach. Other options are listed in the [Easter Island excursion catalog](/chile/easter-island/) and the [Culture and History](/interests/culture-and-history/) section.

## Frequently asked questions about the southern coast of Rapa Nui

### How many moai stand at Ahu Tongariki?

The restored platform has **15 moai**.

### Is the picnic at Anakena included?

Yes. This specific excursion includes a private picnic at the beach.

### Can I swim?

The itinerary allows time for swimming at Anakena, provided actual conditions are suitable.

### How long does the excursion last?

The route is designed as a full-day trip; the length of individual stops depends on the agreed schedule.
